papers.title: Randomness Certification from Statistically Hiding Commitments
papers.authors: Ilya Merkulov; Rotem Arnon
papers.problem: What cryptographic assumption lets a classical verifier certify randomness from a single untrusted quantum device, secure against quantum side information?
papers.result: A statistically hiding bit commitment that is computationally binding against quantum senders suffices; stronger notions such as collapse-binding are not needed. Consequently, post-quantum one-way permutations suffice. Trapdoor claw-free functions give an efficient verifier, and the quantum random-oracle model gives certification with no further assumption but an inefficient verifier.
papers.significance: Separates what security needs (hiding and binding) from what efficient verification needs (a trapdoor to recover unique openings), and shows that a proof of quantumness is not automatically a randomness certificate.
papers.limitations: The honest prover gets past the hashing step only with probability about \(1/(10m)\), so the single-round gap is inverse-polynomial. Whether arbitrary post-quantum one-way functions suffice is open, and the random-oracle verifier uses exhaustive search.
description: A Bell test certifies that outputs are random, even to an adversary holding quantum side information, because spatially separated devices cannot learn each other’s inputs. A single device sees the whole transcript, so the separation must come from computational hardness instead. In the computational Bell framework, a virtual input \(x=\xi(t)\) is a function of the transcript that the device cannot efficiently compute, and a virtual output \(a=\alpha(t)\) is defined alongside it. A fresh challenge \(y\) and the device’s answer \(b\) complete a CHSH round, accepted when \(a\oplus b=xy\).

The paper distinguishes two kinds of hiding. If \(x\) is hidden from efficient classical predictors, a classical device cannot win with probability above \(3/4\) plus a negligible amount, so winning more proves quantumness. Randomness needs more. If a quantum device could recover \(x\) from its leftover quantum state, it could tailor its answer to \(x\) and win without the incompatible measurements that force uncertainty. The virtual input must therefore be hidden from quantum predictors that hold the residual state.

The protocol builds on a construction of Morimae and Yamakawa. The prover runs the commitment’s sender in superposition. Pairwise-independent hashing isolates one valid opening for each bit, leaving \(\ket0\ket{x_0}+\ket1\ket{x_1}\). The verifier sends random strings \(r_0,r_1\), and the prover computes inner products and measures in the Hadamard basis. This leaves a BB84 state whose basis is the virtual input \(\xi=(x_0\cdot r_0)\oplus(x_1\cdot r_1)\). Measuring \(M_y=(Z+(-1)^yX)/\sqrt2\) wins CHSH with probability \(\cos^2(\pi/8)\approx0.854\). Theorem 1 shows that \(\xi\) is hidden from quantum predictors if the commitment is binding against quantum senders.

Theorem 2 then bounds the conditional entropy of the answer, \(H(B\mid T,Y,E)\ge c_0-O(\sqrt\varepsilon)-\mathrm{negl}(\lambda)/\gamma\), when the device wins with probability \(\omega^*-\varepsilon\). A direct proof via Jordan’s lemma and entropic uncertainty relations is also given. Entropy accumulation extends this to a sequential protocol with smooth min-entropy guarantees. The two instantiations isolate the role of the trapdoor. Claw-free functions let the verifier recover the unique openings efficiently. The hash commitment \(c=\mathcal G(b\|r)\) in the random-oracle model satisfies hiding and binding, but its verifier must search exhaustively.

methods.technique: Hide a BB84 basis inside two commitment openings
methods.explanation: The prover holds a superposition of the two openings of one commitment. Random inner products plus a Hadamard measurement leave a single qubit whose basis is an unpredictable bit of the transcript.
math: After the verifier sends \(r_0,r_1\), the honest state is \(\ket0\ket{x_0}\ket{x_0\cdot r_0}+\ket1\ket{x_1}\ket{x_1\cdot r_1}\). The bit register is uncomputed, since \(b\) is determined by \(x\). Measuring the opening register in the Hadamard basis uses \(H^{\otimes\ell}\ket x=2^{-\ell/2}\sum_d(-1)^{d\cdot x}\ket d\). Outcome \(d\) leaves \[\ket{\psi_t}\propto\ket{x_0\cdot r_0}+(-1)^{d\cdot(x_0\oplus x_1)}\ket{x_1\cdot r_1}.\] If the two inner products agree (\(\xi=0\)), this is the \(Z\) eigenstate \(\ket{x_0\cdot r_0}\). If they differ (\(\xi=1\)), it is an \(X\) eigenstate with sign bit \(d\cdot(x_0\oplus x_1)\). These are the virtual outputs \(a\) of Definition 3.2.

CHSH check (editorial). For \(\xi=0\) the target is \(b=a\); measuring along \((Z\pm X)/\sqrt2\), at \(45^\circ\) to \(Z\), gives it with probability \(\cos^2(\pi/8)\). For \(\xi=1\) the target is \(b=a\oplus y\): \(M_0\) leans toward \(+X\), so \(b=a\), while \(M_1\) leans toward \(-X\), so \(b=a\oplus1\). Each case wins with probability \(\cos^2(\pi/8)\approx0.854>3/4\).
methods.transfer: Measuring in the Hadamard basis a register that holds one of two strings collapses the remaining qubit’s phase to the parity \(d\cdot(x_0\oplus x_1)\). Combined with public random inner products, this prepares a BB84 state remotely whose basis the preparer cannot know. It works from any primitive that yields a coherent pair of preimages: commitments, two-to-one functions, claw-free pairs.

methods.technique: Turn a predictor into two openings
methods.explanation: Security reduces predicting the virtual input to breaking binding. A predictor for \(\xi\) is converted, via a quantum Goldreich–Levin procedure, into a sender that outputs both openings of one commitment.
math: The virtual input is an inner product of a secret with public randomness: \[\xi=(x_0\cdot r_0)\oplus(x_1\cdot r_1)=(x_0\|x_1)\cdot(r_0\|r_1).\] The Goldreich–Levin theorem states that if \(w\cdot r\) can be guessed with probability \(\tfrac12+\eta\) over uniform \(r\), then \(w\) can be recovered in time \(\mathrm{poly}(\ell,1/\eta)\). Editorial intuition for the easy case: \(w\cdot r\oplus w\cdot(r\oplus e_i)=w_i\), so two guesses with error rate below \(1/4\) give each bit \(w_i\) by majority vote. The full theorem handles any non-negligible advantage, and the Adcock–Cleve version applies to quantum predictors.

Recovering \(x_0\|x_1\) gives classical openings of the same commitment to both 0 and 1 in a single execution. That is exactly the event that computational binding against quantum senders forbids, so \(\Pr[\text{predict }\xi]\le\tfrac12+\mathrm{negl}(\lambda)\) whenever the protocol continues with non-negligible probability. The proof never needs the committed bit to be fixed after the commit phase. This is why collapse-binding and sum-binding are not required.
methods.transfer: To prove that a hidden bit is unpredictable, write it as an inner product of secret strings with fresh public randomness. Goldreich–Levin then turns any predictor into an extractor for the secrets, and security reduces to the hardness of producing them: binding, claw-freeness or collision resistance. Check which form of the underlying assumption the extraction actually contradicts; it may be weaker than expected.

papers.title: Conservation in Every Quantum Measurement Outcome?
papers.authors: E. Okon; D. Sudarsky; M. Wiedemann
papers.problem: Does including the system that prepared a superposition restore a conservation law in every individual measurement outcome, as Collins and Popescu have proposed?
papers.result: The authors argue that it does not, in the sense claimed. The need for a physical preparer is postulated rather than derived from the relativity of angle. The preparer never holds a definite value, so what the mechanism restores is a shifted probability distribution. A preparation that conserves one observable can disturb a noncommuting one. For energy, the preparation interaction breaks the additivity the bookkeeping relies on.
papers.significance: Separates two claims that are easy to run together. A conservation-respecting preparation can leave compensating correlations with the preparer, which is true. Conservation outcome by outcome would also need every superposition to carry such correlations, which has not been shown.
papers.limitations: This is a critique, not a theorem. The spin-\(\tfrac12\) counterexample uses a one-spin preparer, for which the prepared spin is maximally mixed, so it tests the bookkeeping rather than the near-pure regime of the original proposal. The energy objection is stated qualitatively; the size of the interaction term is not estimated.
description: Collins and Popescu (Quantum, 2025) model preparation explicitly. A preparer \(P\) starts in \(\ket{\Phi}_P\) and the system in a reference eigenstate \(\ket0_S\) of a conserved quantity. A conserving unitary produces \(\sum_n\alpha(n)\ket{\Phi-n}_P\ket n_S\), in which every amount \(n\) gained by the system is matched by a shift \(-n\) of the preparer. A measurement with outcome \(k\) leaves \(\ket{\Phi-k}_P\ket k_S\), so each branch has the initial total. For the system to look almost pure, the shifted preparer states must overlap almost perfectly, which requires a preparer broad in the conserved quantity. A grand-preparer that made \(P\) keeps its marginal distribution unchanged, so the accounting closes on \(S\) and \(P\).

Is a preparer necessary? The proposal argues that the relative phases of a superposition of angular-momentum states encode an angle, and an absolute angle is meaningless, so a physical frame must exist and must be the preparer. The authors accept the premise but not the inference. Angle being defined only relative to a frame is a fact about how the theory represents states; it does not require a further material body. A single Galilean particle has no absolute position, yet nobody concludes that a one-particle universe is ill-defined. Applied consistently, the inference also regresses: the system and preparer together need a frame, and so on without end.

Granting the frame, a second gap remains between viability and necessity. Collins and Popescu show that one interaction can prepare the state while leaving the compensating correlations. Their account needs every admissible preparation history to contain such an interaction somewhere, and this is postulated. Even then, the preparer is never in an eigenstate of the conserved quantity, before or after the measurement. What shifts by \(-k\) is its distribution, so the result is statistical conservation conditioned on the outcome. Requiring each preparer to look pure to the next forces widths \(\sigma_S\ll\sigma_P\ll\sigma_{GP}\ll\cdots\) up the chain.

Two further objections concern scope. A two-spin example shows that a preparation conserving total \(S_z\) changes the distribution of total \(S_x\), so the bookkeeping must pick one of several noncommuting conserved quantities. Appealing to the measuring device for the others undercuts the proposal’s own motivation. For energy, the preparation needs \(H_{\mathrm{tot}}=H_S+H_P+H_{\mathrm{int}}\), so opposite shifts of the subsystem energies do not by themselves establish conservation. Whether a localized form of statistical conservation is the right goal is left open.

methods.technique: Test a conservation mechanism against the whole symmetry group
methods.explanation: The authors check whether a preparation built to conserve \(S_z\) also conserves \(S_x\). It does not, which shows that the mechanism is tied to one observable.
math: Take a preparer spin and a system spin starting in \(\ket{+z}_P\ket{-z}_S\). A total-\(S_z\)-conserving preparation can produce \[\ket{\Psi'}=\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\bigl(\ket{-z}_P\ket{+z}_S+\ket{+z}_P\ket{-z}_S\bigr)=\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\bigl(\ket{+x}_P\ket{+x}_S-\ket{-x}_P\ket{-x}_S\bigr).\] In units of \(\hbar/2\), the total \(S_x\) of the initial state takes the values \(+2,0,-2\) with probabilities \(\tfrac14,\tfrac12,\tfrac14\), while the final state gives \(+2\) and \(-2\) with probability \(\tfrac12\) each and never \(0\).

Why no fix is possible here (editorial). The initial state splits evenly between the singlet and the triplet \(m=0\) state: \(\ket{+z}\ket{-z}=\bigl(\ket{T_0}+\ket{S_0}\bigr)/\sqrt2\). The final state is \(\ket{T_0}\), with no singlet weight. A unitary that conserves all three components of total spin commutes with total \(\mathbf S^2\) and so preserves the weight in each total-spin sector. A change of singlet weight from \(\tfrac12\) to \(0\) therefore certifies that some component of total spin was not conserved. Both distributions above were checked numerically.
methods.transfer: When a mechanism is designed to conserve one generator of a symmetry, decompose the initial and final states into the group’s irreducible sectors. A process that conserves every generator preserves each sector’s weight, so any change in sector weights is an immediate certificate that some conserved quantity has been violated.

methods.technique: Overlap factors set how broad a hidden partner must be
methods.explanation: The authors make the near-purity requirement quantitative with a Gaussian preparer and apply it recursively up the chain of preparers.
math: Tracing out the preparer from \(\sum_n\alpha(n)\ket{\Phi-n}_P\ket n_S\) gives (editorial) \[\rho_S=\sum_{n,m}\alpha(n)\alpha(m)^*\braket{\Phi-m}{\Phi-n}\,\ket n\bra m,\] so each coherence is multiplied by an overlap of shifted preparer states. If the preparer amplitudes are \(\Phi(n)\propto e^{-n^2/(4\sigma_P^2)}\), so that its distribution has width \(\sigma_P\), then completing the square in \((n-a)^2+(n-b)^2=2\bigl(n-\tfrac{a+b}2\bigr)^2+\tfrac{(a-b)^2}2\) gives \[\braket{\Phi-a}{\Phi-b}\approx\exp\!\Bigl[-\frac{(a-b)^2}{8\sigma_P^2}\Bigr],\] the paper’s Eq. (12).

Near-purity needs this factor close to \(1\) for every populated pair, so \(\sigma_P\gg\sigma_S:=\max|n-m|\). The preparer is itself a superposition of width \(\sigma_P\), and the same argument applied to it requires \(\sigma_{GP}\gg\sigma_P\). Recursion gives \(\sigma_S\ll\sigma_P\ll\sigma_{GP}\ll\cdots\) and conjugate widths \(\Delta_P\gg\Delta_{GP}\gg\cdots\): ever more idealized reference systems.
methods.transfer: Any account that hides bookkeeping in a partner system, such as a reference frame, a which-path memory or an environment, faces the same trade-off. The partner must be correlated enough to carry the record yet nearly uninformative so that the system still looks pure. Write the reduced state, read off the overlap factor, and ask whether the partner can satisfy the same requirement it imposes.

papers.title: An entanglement band structure for general multiqubit states
papers.authors: Chon-Fai Kam
papers.problem: Majorana pictured a symmetric multiqubit state as points on the sphere. Can a comparable geometric picture be given for general states, whose entanglement classes form continuous families?
papers.result: Projecting one qubit onto a direction \(\mathbf n\) leaves a conditional state of the others. Its entanglement invariants are the eigenvalues, called bands, of a non-Hermitian matrix \(L(u)\). For five qubits there are four bands, which meet at 24 exceptional points where the conditional state changes entanglement family. Together they form one Riemann surface of genus nine, which fixes the five-qubit entanglement class up to finitely many choices.
papers.significance: Gives general multiqubit entanglement a geometry with measurable features. The exceptional points arise from conditioning a pure state, with no gain or loss, and circling one exchanges two bands, which tomography of the remaining qubits can detect.
papers.limitations: The curve classifies states only at five qubits. From seven qubits on, operations that entangle qubits within a block leave it unchanged. The construction degenerates for states symmetric under exchanging a pair, where one band vanishes identically. The count of realized eigenvector-sign patterns is numerical, and the shot-noise estimates for observing an exchange are simulations.
description: Three qubits can be genuinely entangled in two inequivalent ways, GHZ and W. Two states count as equivalent when stochastic local operations and classical communication (SLOCC) convert one into the other with nonzero probability. From four qubits on, the classes form continuous families: generic five-qubit classes depend on \(2^5-1-3\cdot5=16\) complex parameters. For symmetric states Majorana’s construction gives a complete picture. The state is fixed by \(n\) points on the Bloch sphere, local operations applied equally to every qubit move the points by Möbius maps, and symmetries are symmetries of the points. Points on the sphere modulo Möbius maps carry only \(n-3\) parameters, however, so they cannot describe general states.

The paper projects a single qubit instead of all of them. With stereographic coordinate \(t=\tan(\theta/2)e^{-i\varphi}\) and \(u=(1,t)\), projecting the fifth qubit leaves amplitudes \(R(u)_{ab}=\sum_s\psi_{abs}u_s\), where \(a\) labels qubits 1 and 2 and \(b\) labels qubits 3 and 4. For almost every direction the conditional state lies in the generic four-qubit family \(G_{abcd}\), and \(a^2,b^2,c^2,d^2\) are the eigenvalues of \[L(u)=R(u)\,G\,R(u)^{\mathsf T}G,\qquad G=\sigma_y\otimes\sigma_y.\] These four functions of the direction are the bands, by analogy with energy bands over a Brillouin zone. Choosing which qubit to project and how to split the rest into pairs gives fifteen band sets for a five-qubit state.

Two bands meet where two coefficients coincide up to sign. There \(L\) acquires a \(2\times2\) Jordan block and the conditional state drops into the family \(L_{abc_2}\). These exceptional points are the zeros of the discriminant of \(L\), a polynomial of degree 24 in \(t\). Circling one exchanges the two bands, and the 24 exchanges generate all permutations, so the four bands are sheets of one curve \(C\) of genus nine. Since \(\det L=(\det R)^2\), the curve touches \(w=0\) without crossing it. Counting parameters, 24 coefficients minus 4 fixed by this identity, 3 Möbius maps and 1 scale, leaves exactly 16, matching the classes. The curve does not fix the eigenvectors: their signs are \(\mathbb Z_2\) Berry phases on the curve’s 18 independent loops. About a quarter of the \(2^{18}\) patterns occur numerically, and a linear test decides whether two states with equal band coefficients are equivalent.

Symmetric states split the curve into pieces. The GHZ state has bands \(0\) and \(u_0u_1/2\), each twice. The W state has all bands zero, since every conditional state lies in the nullcone. The ring cluster state has bands \(\pm8it^2\) and \(\pm8i\). The number of qubits fixes a non-Hermitian symmetry class: \(n\equiv1\pmod4\) gives class AI\(^\dagger\), \(n\equiv3\pmod4\) forces Kramers-doubled bands, and even \(n\) pairs \(w\) with \(-w\). A simulated experiment with 80 shots per Pauli setting, about \(4\times10^5\) shots in all, recovers the exchange around one exceptional point in 96% of runs. Whether the curves of all projected qubits and splits together classify states beyond five qubits is open.

methods.technique: Read SLOCC invariants from a holomorphic matrix pencil
methods.explanation: Contracting the conditional amplitudes with the invariant form of SL(2) gives a matrix whose spectrum is unchanged by local operations on the four remaining qubits.
math: For a two-qubit state \(\phi\), \(\phi^{\mathsf T}G\phi=-2(\phi_{00}\phi_{11}-\phi_{01}\phi_{10})\), minus twice the determinant of its coefficient matrix. A local operation \(X=M_1\otimes M_2\) with \(\det M_i=1\) satisfies \(X^{\mathsf T}GX=G\), because \(M^{\mathsf T}\sigma_yM=\det(M)\,\sigma_y\). Hence \(X^{-1}=GX^{\mathsf T}G\), and \(R\mapsto XR\) sends \(L\mapsto XRGR^{\mathsf T}X^{\mathsf T}G=XLX^{-1}\). On the other pair, \(R\mapsto RY^{\mathsf T}\) leaves \(L\) unchanged, since \(Y^{\mathsf T}GY=G\).

An operation \(Z\) on the projected qubit replaces \(u\) by \(Z^{\mathsf T}u\), a Möbius map of the sphere; \(L\) is quadratic in \(u\), so all bands rescale together. Since \(\det G=1\), \(\det L=(\det R)^2\). Editorial check: for a random five-qubit state, the bands were unchanged under random \(\mathrm{SL}(2)^{\otimes4}\) operations, the identity \(\det L=(\det R)^2\) and the relation \(L^{\mathsf T}G=GL\) held, and the three splits gave equal \(\operatorname{tr}L\).
methods.transfer: When a group acts on a tensor leg by leg, contract with the group’s invariant bilinear form to get a matrix with an invariant spectrum. Letting one leg depend linearly on a parameter turns these invariants into holomorphic functions, so their degeneracies become isolated points that can be counted rather than tuned.

methods.technique: Count exceptional points and the genus from the discriminant
methods.explanation: The degree of the discriminant fixes how many exceptional points there are, and the Riemann–Hurwitz formula turns that count into the topology of the band surface.
math: The coefficients \(\chi_j\) of \(\det(w\mathbb I-L(u))=\sum_j(-1)^j\chi_jw^{m-j}\) are homogeneous of degree \(2j\) in \(u\). Each factor \((w_i-w_j)^2\) of the discriminant has degree four, so the discriminant has degree \(b=4\binom m2=2m(m-1)\), which is 24 for \(m=4\). Near a simple zero \(t_0\) two bands behave as \(w\approx w_0\pm c\sqrt{t-t_0}\); one loop sends \(\sqrt{\cdot}\to-\sqrt{\cdot}\) and swaps them. For an \(m\)-sheeted cover of the sphere with \(b\) simple branch points, Riemann–Hurwitz gives \(2g-2=-2m+b\). Hence (editorial algebra) \(g=m^2-2m+1=(m-1)^2\), which is \(9\) at five qubits.

Why the meetings are isolated (editorial): Hermitian bands need three real conditions to meet (von Neumann–Wigner), but a holomorphic family needs only one complex equation, the vanishing of the discriminant, so generic degeneracies sit at points. Editorial check: for a random five-qubit state the discriminant had degree 24 with 24 roots, and tracking the bands once around one root permuted exactly two of them.
methods.transfer: For any matrix family that depends holomorphically on a parameter, the discriminant’s degree counts the exceptional points and Riemann–Hurwitz gives the topology of the eigenvalue surface, without diagonalizing anywhere. Encircling a predicted point and watching two eigenvalues exchange is a robust experimental test, because it depends only on whether the loop encloses the point.

papers.title: Injection is all you need: parallel universal logic in high-rate concatenated self-dual codes
papers.authors: Joseph Sullivan; David Amaro; Michael A. Perlin
papers.problem: High-rate codes store many logical qubits per block but make it hard to act on a chosen subset. How can they run parallel, addressable, universal logic?
papers.result: In concatenated self-dual codes with transversal global \(H\) and \(S\), any logical Clifford is injected by consuming at most 9 CSS resource states. \(T\) gates on any subset need one \(\ket H^{\otimes K}\) magic state and one CSS state, so a circuit of \(T\)-depth \(D_T\) needs at most \(12D_T\) resource states. A Hadamard parity check repeated at each concatenation level gives magic states whose undetected error is \(O(p^{2^L})\). In simulations at \(p=5\times10^{-4}\), this concatenated cultivation needed about ten times less spacetime than surface-code cultivation for the two distance-4 codes.
papers.significance: Replaces addressability built into the code with teleportation of prepared resource states, which also performs error correction and removes leakage as it runs.
papers.limitations: Magic-state performance is simulated with a Clifford proxy (\(\ket+\) in place of \(\ket H\), CX in place of CH). Discard rates are high: 41–87% for magic states and up to 96% for the largest CNOT resource state. The decoder is a lookup table that will not scale. For [[96,14,6]] the table supports only a factor of about two over surface-code cultivation, because the surface-code cost there is a lower bound. Costs are per resource state, not per algorithm.
description: High-rate codes suffer from an addressability problem: acting on a chosen subset of the logical qubits in a block is hard, so logically independent gates are serialized. The paper avoids building addressable gates into the code. Almost every gate is instead injected by teleportation, consuming a resource state prepared in advance. The codes are concatenations of self-dual CSS codes with equivalent logicals (SWEL), for which \(H^{\otimes n}\) implements logical \(\bar H^{\otimes k}\) and \(S^{\otimes n}\) implements \(\bar S^{\otimes k}\) up to \(Z\) gates. Every self-dual CSS code of odd length is SWEL. Injection doubles as error correction: Knill-type gadgets measure the full syndrome, Steane-type gadgets part of it.

For Cliffords, the Bruhat decomposition writes any \(k\)-qubit Clifford as nine layers of types (CX, S, CX, S, H, S, CX, S, CX). An earlier scheme injected each layer from a generally non-CSS resource state made by distillation, which for a single copy needs a factory of \(n(d+1)^2\) qubits. Theorem 1 shows that the global \(\bar H^{\otimes k}\) and \(\bar S^{\otimes k}\) gates reduce every layer to CSS resource states. These are prepared without distillation by the flag-at-origin method. For [[36,4,4]], the depth-optimized CNOT resource state uses 264 qubits, against a 3600-qubit distillation factory.

For the non-Clifford part, \(T\) gates on a chosen subset \(\mathbf t\) come from \(T^{\otimes\mathbf t}\ket+^{\otimes k}=(SHSH)^{\otimes k}\ket{H,\mathbf t}\). Here \(\ket{H,\mathbf t}\) holds \(\ket H\) where \(t_j=1\) and \(\ket0\) elsewhere, and it is made from \(\ket H^{\otimes k}\) by consuming one \(H^{\otimes\mathbf t}\ket0^{\otimes k}\) state. Because \(H^{\otimes k}\) is transversal and stabilizes \(\ket H^{\otimes k}\), it can be measured fault-tolerantly to flag faulty preparations (zero-level distillation). A single parity check sees only the parity of the faulty factors, which caps it at \(O(p^2)\). Concatenated cultivation repeats the check at every level, where the level-2 parity runs across different level-1 blocks. This drives undetected errors to \(O(p^4)\) at two levels and \(O(p^{2^L})\) in general.

A code of distance \(D\) can only use that suppression up to its correction capability: the effective rate is \(O(p^{\min\{2^L,\,t+2\}})\) with \(t=\lfloor(D-1)/2\rfloor\), when decoder rejections are used for even \(D\). Simulations at \(p=5\times10^{-4}\) give logical errors \(8.3\times10^{-9}\) for [[36,4,4]] (112 qubits, 41% discarded), \(2.2\times10^{-8}\) for [[48,8,4]], and \(1.1\times10^{-10}\) for [[96,14,6]] (256 qubits, 87% discarded). The spacetime costs are \(1.4\times10^4\), \(2.2\times10^4\) and \(3.2\times10^5\), against \(1.6\times10^5\), \(3.2\times10^5\) and more than \(6.0\times10^5\) for surface-code cultivation at matched batch error. End-to-end algorithm costs remain to be estimated.

methods.technique: Reduce every Clifford layer to CSS resource states
methods.explanation: Global transversal \(H\) and \(S\) conjugate the resource states for addressable phase and Hadamard layers into CSS states, which can be prepared without distillation.
math: Gate teleportation consumes \(\ket{\Phi,U}\), the result of applying \(U\) to one half of \(k\) Bell pairs; measuring in the Bell basis applies \(UX^{\mathbf z}Z^{\mathbf x}\) to the data. For Clifford \(U\) the byproduct \(UPU^\dagger\) is a Pauli, corrected for free. For an S layer the needed state is \(S^{\otimes\mathbf s}\ket+^{\otimes k}\simeq(HS^\dagger)^{\otimes k}H^{\otimes\mathbf s}\ket0^{\otimes k}\). Check per qubit (editorial): \(HS^\dagger\ket0=\ket+\), and \(HS^\dagger\ket+=\tfrac{1-i}2(\ket0+i\ket1)\simeq S\ket+\). So a CSS state followed by a global gate supplies every addressable S layer.

For an H layer, write \(H=XS_Y\) with \(S_Y=e^{-i\pi Y/4}\simeq(SH)S(HS^\dagger)\). Then \[H^{\otimes\mathbf h}\simeq X^{\otimes\mathbf h}(SH)^{\otimes k}S^{\otimes\mathbf h}(HS^\dagger)^{\otimes k},\] so an addressable Hadamard layer costs one addressable S layer plus global gates and Paulis. Both identities were checked numerically up to global phase.
methods.transfer: If a code offers fault-tolerant global gates and cheap preparation of one class of states, look for decompositions in which global gates conjugate every needed resource state into that class. This moves addressing out of the gates and into state preparation, where flags or verification are easier to apply.

methods.technique: Hadamard-parity flags, and why one parity stalls at second order
methods.explanation: Measuring the transversal stabilizer \(H^{\otimes k}\) of a magic-state batch catches single faults but misses pairs; concatenation supplies independent groupings that catch pairs too.
math: \(\ket H\) is the \(+1\) eigenstate of \(H=(X+Z)/\sqrt2\). Since \(Y\) anticommutes with \(X\) and \(Z\), \(YHY=-H\) and \(Y\ket H=\ket{-H}\), so one \(Y\) flips the measured parity. A single \(X\) or \(Z\) gives \(|\bra H X\ket H|^2=\tfrac12\) (editorial): with probability \(\tfrac12\) it is flagged, and otherwise the projection returns that qubit to \(\ket H\). Two errors can both flip, for example \(Y_1Y_2\ket H\ket H=\ket{-H}\ket{-H}\), which has parity \(+1\) and passes unseen. This is why the paper requires every single fault to act as one logical \(X\), one \(Z\), or an odd number of \(Y\)s, and why one parity check caps the error at \(O(p^2)\).

In \(C_1\circ C_2\) each level-1 qubit of a \(C_1\) block sits in a different \(C_2\) block, so the level-2 parities \(H^{\otimes n_2}\) group qubits differently from the level-1 parities. A pair that cancels inside one level-1 parity is split between different level-2 parities and caught there, giving \(O(p^4)\); induction gives \(O(p^{2^L})\) for errors with no syndrome. Editorial check: \(Y_1Y_2\ket{HH}\) passes the parity, and a single \(X\) passes with probability \(\tfrac12\).
methods.transfer: A transversal operator that stabilizes a batch of magic states is a free fault-tolerant check, but a single global parity sees only how many factors flipped. To get past second order, measure parities over several independent groupings of the same qubits; the levels of a concatenated code provide them naturally.

papers.title: Finite Classification of Transversal Diagonal Gates Beyond Stabilizer Codes
papers.authors: Xi He; Chao Zhang; Shilin Huang; Bei Zeng
papers.problem: Code-preserving diagonal phases of general (nonadditive) qubit codes can vary continuously. Can the transversal diagonal gates of such codes still be classified exhaustively?
papers.result: Yes, at fixed code parameters. For a code of distance at least two, every projective logical action of a transversal diagonal gate has a physical representative of finite order \(q\), with \(m\mid q\) and \(q\) bounded in terms of \(n\) and \(K\) alone; \(q\le9\) for six qubits at distance three. For exact ((6,2,3)) codes, 66 candidate symmetry classes reduce to 15 realizable ones, with diagonal logical groups \(C_2\), \(C_3\) or \(C_5\). The order-five code is unique up to local unitaries and qubit permutations. It is also the shortest distance-3 qubit code whose transversal logical group cannot be conjugated into the Clifford group.
papers.significance: Turns the subset-sum–linear-programming (SSLP) construction into a complete classification procedure, with no stabilizer or additivity assumption. Continuous families of nonadditive codes can therefore be searched exhaustively for transversal symmetries.
papers.limitations: Diagonality refers to one fixed product basis, so noncommuting transversal generators that cannot be diagonalized together are not covered. A code-level classification is complete only in the order-five sector, and two of the fifteen weight-enumerator sets remain open. The case-by-case proofs and Lean verification were produced by AI agents and audited by the authors; the structural theorems are the authors’ own.
description: Transversal gates act qubit by qubit and so do not spread faults, but by the Eastin–Knill theorem they cannot be universal on a code that detects single-qubit errors. Stabilizer codes have finite Pauli descriptions that make classification tractable. Nonadditive codes come in continuous families, and a transversal symmetry adds continuous phases of its own. The SSLP method fixes a finite-order diagonal gate \(D(a;q)=\bigotimes_j\operatorname{diag}(1,\omega_q^{a_j})\), \(\omega_q=e^{2\pi i/q}\). Basis strings then fall into sectors \(S_b=\{x:a\cdot x\equiv b\pmod q\}\), and the logical eigenvectors must live in distinct sectors. The diagonal Knill–Laflamme (KL) conditions become a linear program on squared amplitudes, and the remaining conditions an exact algebraic completion.

Two gaps stood between that method and completeness. A code-preserving diagonal gate can have irrational phases, and so infinite physical order. And the least physical order realizing a logical action can exceed its logical order. Theorem III.2 closes the first gap using only the single-qubit conditions \(PZ_jP=\lambda_jP\). Preservation is an integer-linear condition on the phases. Directions in its real kernel act as logical scalars, and a rational section lemma replaces any solution by one with a fixed denominator. The diagonal logical group is therefore finite abelian, with finite-order representatives satisfying \(m\mid q\). A seven-qubit example shows the second gap is real: a logical action of order 6 whose physical representatives all have order divisible by 12.

Theorem III.4 shows that every such code has an SSLP normal form, and that every exact completion of SSLP data is a code. Theorem III.9 bounds the needed order. All logical eigenspaces share the same first moment \(\mu\), so the phases solve a binary linear system, and the Smith normal form bounds its denominators: \(q\le\beta_{n+\ell-1}\), with \(\beta_5,\ldots,\beta_9=5,9,18,42,120\). At distance three with one logical qubit, the second moments force the two supports to share an affine span, sharpening the bound to \(q\le\beta_n\), which is 9 for six qubits.

For exact ((6,2,3)) codes the search gives 66 candidate classes. Exact no-go proofs exclude 51, and explicit codes realize 15: 11 of logical order 2, 3 of order 3, and 1 of order 5. In the order-five code, \(D(a^\star;5)\) with \(a^\star=(1,1,1,1,2,3)\) acts as \(\operatorname{diag}(1,\zeta^4)\), \(\zeta=e^{2\pi i/5}\). Every code with this symmetry is equivalent to it, and since it has \(A_1=0\), no shorter code can carry an order-five transversal action. Exact weight enumerators are determined for 13 of the 15 classes. The case analysis was produced by agents using TeXRA with GPT-5.6 and checked in Lean.

methods.technique: Strip continuous phases that act only as logical scalars
methods.explanation: Single-qubit error detection makes every kernel direction of the phase constraints act as a scalar on the code, so continuous phase families collapse to a finite set of logical actions.
math: \(D(t)\) multiplies \(\ket x\) by \(e^{2\pi i\,x\cdot t}\), so \((D(t)PD(t)^\dagger)_{xy}=e^{2\pi i(x-y)\cdot t}P_{xy}\), and the code is preserved if and only if \((x-y)\cdot t\in\mathbb Z\) whenever \(P_{xy}\ne0\). If \((x-y)\cdot h=0\) for all such pairs, then \(H_h=\sum_jh_jN_j\), with \(N_j=(I-Z_j)/2\), commutes with \(P\). Detection gives \(PN_jP=\mu_jP\), so \(H_hP=PH_hP=(h\cdot\mu)P\) and \(D(h)P=e^{2\pi i\,h\cdot\mu}P\). Subtracting such an \(h\) changes the logical action only by a scalar. With \(B=A^{\mathsf T}A\), a rational \(G\) with \(BGB=B\) and \(Q_AG\) integral, \(a=Q_AGA^{\mathsf T}(At)\) satisfies \(A(t-a/Q_A)=0\), because \(\ker A^{\mathsf T}A=\ker A\).

Example III.3: \(\theta(t)=\tfrac1{12}(3,3,3,3,4,4,4)+t(1,-1,0,0,1,-1,0)\) preserves a seven-qubit distance-2 code for every real \(t\), with logical action \(\operatorname{diag}(1,e^{2\pi i/6})\). For irrational \(t\) the physical gate never repeats. Any finite-order representative has phase \(a/4\) with \(a\) odd on qubit 3 and \(b/3\) with \(b\equiv1\) on qubit 7, so \(12\mid q\) although \(m=6\). Editorial check: at \(t=0\) and \(t=\sqrt2/7\) the gate preserves both codewords with relative phase exactly \(1/6\) turn, and \(\langle Z_1Z_2\rangle\) is \(1\) and \(-\tfrac13\) on the two codewords, confirming distance two.
methods.transfer: When a symmetry search has continuous parameters, find the directions that act trivially on the object of interest and quotient them out. What remains is a rational lattice problem whose denominators a Smith normal form can bound. Do not assume the smallest physical order equals the logical order; search over its multiples.

methods.technique: Subset-sum sectors and moment matching as a staged filter
methods.explanation: A diagonal gate sorts basis strings by phase; codewords must live in single sectors, and the diagonal error conditions become cheap linear constraints before the hard amplitude equations are solved.
math: With \(\ket{0_L}\) supported in \(S_0\) and \(\ket{1_L}\) in \(S_{q/m}\), off-diagonal elements of every diagonal Pauli \(Z_J\) vanish automatically. The diagonal conditions \(\sum_xp_0(x)\prod_{j\in J}(1-2x_j)=\sum_yp_1(y)\prod_{j\in J}(1-2y_j)\) for \(|J|<d\) are equivalent, via \(z_j=1-2x_j\), to equal binary moments up to degree \(d-1\). At distance three this means \(\phi_2(x)=(1,x_i,x_ix_j)\) must have a common average, a linear-programming test: the convex hulls of \(\phi_2(S_0)\) and \(\phi_2(S_{q/m})\) must intersect. Passing it is necessary, not sufficient, since the \(X\)- and \(Y\)-type conditions remain.

Editorial check on the order-five code with \(a^\star=(1,1,1,1,2,3)\): the strings of \(\ket{\psi_0}\) have subset sums \(0\), \(3+2\) and \(2+3\), all \(\equiv0\pmod5\). Those of \(\ket{\psi_1}\) have sums \(4\), \(4+5\), \(1+3\) and \(2+2\), all \(\equiv4\pmod5\), so the gate acts as \(\operatorname{diag}(1,\zeta^4)\). Numerically, all Paulis of weight at most two satisfy the KL conditions to within \(2\times10^{-16}\).
methods.transfer: To search for codes with a prescribed diagonal symmetry, stage the problem: discrete supports from the gate’s phase sectors, then convex moment conditions, then the exact complex equations. The cheap stages prune most candidates, and the staging does not depend on stabilizer structure.

papers.title: Tight Bounds on the Randomized Communication Complexity of Vector-in-Subspace
papers.authors: Chengu Wang
papers.problem: One quantum message of \(\lceil\log_2n\rceil\) qubits solves Vector-in-Subspace exactly. How many bits does an interactive classical protocol need?
papers.result: \(\Theta(\sqrt n)\) bits. A lower bound of \(\Omega(\sqrt n)\) holds for bounded-error randomized protocols with any number of rounds, matching Raz’s \(O(\sqrt n)\) protocol. It improves the \(\Omega(n^{1/3})\) bound of Klartag and Regev and removes the total-rank restriction in Grupel’s \(\Omega(\sqrt n)\) result.
papers.significance: Settles the size of a standard exponential separation between one-way quantum and interactive classical communication. The proof introduces a cancellation technique, a vanishing complex moment that survives averaging over a protocol’s rectangles, which avoids the dimension dependence of absolute moments.
papers.limitations: The constants are not explicit. The quantum advantage concerns communication only: the matching classical protocol may require substantial local computation. The proof is long and technical, and the author reports using AI tools to develop and check arguments.
description: Alice holds a unit vector \(x\in\mathbb R^n\) and Bob an \(n/2\)-dimensional subspace \(H\), with the promise that \(x\in H\) or \(x\in H^\perp\). Alice can send the state \(\sum_ix_i\ket i\) on \(\lceil\log_2n\rceil\) qubits; Bob measures the projector onto \(H\) and answers correctly with certainty. Classically, Raz’s protocol uses shared random Gaussian vectors: Alice sends the index of the one most correlated with \(x\), which takes \(O(\sqrt n)\) bits. Could interaction do much better?

Earlier bounds left a gap. Gavinsky, Kempe, Kerenidis, Raz and de Wolf separated one-way quantum from one-way classical communication, but their problem is easy with interaction. Klartag and Regev proved \(\Omega(n^{1/3})\) against interactive protocols by studying how a random half-dimensional subspace samples a set on the sphere. A spherical cap shows that their one-subspace estimate is sharp at the cube-root scale. Grupel studied \(H\) and \(H^\perp\) together and obtained \(\Omega(\sqrt n)\) only for protocols whose decisions depend on few linear functionals of Alice’s vector.

A deterministic \(d\)-bit protocol partitions the inputs into at most \(2^d\) rectangles. Averaging over \(H\cap S^{n-1}\) acts on degree-\(2k\) spherical harmonics with eigenvalue \(\mathfrak a_k=(1/2)_k/((n-1)/2)_k\le(2k/(n-1))^k\), and averaging over \(H^\perp\) adds a sign \((-1)^k\). Only odd \(k\) therefore separate the two promises, and high degrees are negligible. The paper lifts the problem to Gaussians: \(x=Y/|Y|\) and \(H\) is the top-half eigenspace of a GOE matrix \(G\). Each level becomes a Wick-ordered polynomial \(F_k(Y,G)\) of \((Y^{\mathsf T}GY)^k\), and the central estimate is \(\mathbb E\bigl|\mathbb E[F_k\mid\mathsf T]\bigr|\le C^kk!\,(d+k^2)^k\) for every partition \(\mathsf T\) into at most \(2^d\) rectangles. Each level then contributes \((Cd/\sqrt n)^k\), which is small when \(d\le c\sqrt n\).

The estimate rests on cancellation before absolute values are taken. With independent copies \(Z,G'\), the variable \(Q=\tfrac12(Y+iZ)^{\mathsf T}(G+iG')(Y+iZ)\) satisfies \(F_k=2^k\mathbb E[Q^k\mid Y,G]\) and \(\mathbb E Q^{2k}=0\). Since the cells together reproduce the full Gaussian law, this zero survives averaging over the partition, though not within any one cell. On each cell, Alice’s conditional law is split into fixed coordinates, which define a real center \(\alpha\), and a sub-Gaussian remainder controlled through signed Wick moments. A short lemma then turns the vanishing even moment into a bound on \(\alpha\) and on the conditional moment.

methods.technique: Complex Gaussian lifts perform the Wick corrections
methods.explanation: Adding an independent imaginary Gaussian turns ordinary powers into Hermite (Wick) polynomials, and phase symmetry makes every holomorphic moment vanish.
math: The Hermite tensor is \(\mathrm{He}_r(y)=\mathbb E_Z(y+iZ)^{\otimes r}\). At the lowest level, with \(w=y+iZ\), \[F_1(y,G)=\mathbb E\bigl[w^{\mathsf T}(G+iG')w\bigr]=y^{\mathsf T}Gy-\mathbb E[Z^{\mathsf T}GZ]=y^{\mathsf T}Gy-\operatorname{tr}G:\] the imaginary part subtracts the self-contraction, and terms linear in \(Z\) or \(G'\) average to zero. Higher levels subtract all contractions in the same way.

Why \(\mathbb EQ^m=0\) (editorial). \(Y+iZ\) is a circularly symmetric complex Gaussian: \(e^{i\varphi}(Y+iZ)\) has the same law for every \(\varphi\), and \(Q\mapsto e^{2i\varphi}Q\). Hence \(\mathbb EQ^m=e^{2im\varphi}\mathbb EQ^m\) for all \(\varphi\), so \(\mathbb EQ^m=0\) for \(m\ge1\), even though \(\mathbb E|Q|^2\) grows with \(n\). A Monte Carlo check at \(n=6\) gave \(\mathbb E[w^{\mathsf T}(G+iG')w]\approx-8.92\) against \(y^{\mathsf T}Gy-\operatorname{tr}G=-8.91\), and \(|\mathbb EQ^2|\approx0.8\) against \(\mathbb E|Q|^2\approx168\).
methods.transfer: To bound a polynomial that should average to zero, write it as the expectation of a holomorphic expression in complex Gaussians. Signed moments then cancel by phase symmetry, while absolute moments would grow with dimension. The device applies wherever Wick or Hermite polynomials appear, including Fourier-growth bounds in other communication and query lower bounds.

methods.technique: A vanishing even moment bounds a real center
methods.explanation: Lemma 4.1 converts the global identity \(\mathbb EQ^{2k}=0\) into control of conditional moments, needing only signed moments of \(Q-\alpha\) about a real center.
math: Let \(\alpha\) be real and \(\mathcal F\)-measurable, \(\kappa_l=\mathbb E[(Q-\alpha)^l\mid\mathcal F]\) with \(\|\kappa_l\|_{2k/l}\le(l\tau)^l\), and \(t=\|\alpha\|_{2k}\). Expanding \(Q^{2k}=\sum_l\binom{2k}l\alpha^{2k-l}(Q-\alpha)^l\) and taking expectations gives \(0=\mathbb E\alpha^{2k}+\sum_{l\ge1}\binom{2k}l\mathbb E[\alpha^{2k-l}\kappa_l]\). Since \(\alpha\) is real, \(\mathbb E\alpha^{2k}=t^{2k}\ge0\), so Hölder gives \[t^{2k}\le\sum_{l=1}^{2k}\binom{2k}l\,t^{2k-l}(l\tau)^l\le\sum_{l=1}^{2k}(2ek\tau)^lt^{2k-l},\] using \(\binom{2k}l\le(2ek/l)^l\).

If \(t>4ek\tau\), the ratio \(r=2ek\tau/t<\tfrac12\) makes the right side \(t^{2k}\sum_{l\ge1}r^l<t^{2k}\), a contradiction; so \(\|\alpha\|_{2k}\le4ek\tau\). Expanding \(Q^k\) the same way gives \(\|\mathbb E[Q^k\mid\mathcal F]\|_2\le(t+k\tau)^k\le(12k\tau)^k\). The bound on \(|Q-\alpha|\) itself, which would carry the dimension, is never needed.
methods.transfer: When a quantity has a known zero moment overall but you need its conditional behaviour on many cells, expand around a real conditional center. Positivity of an even power of a real number turns the global zero into a bound on the center, so long as the signed conditional moments are small.

papers.title: Quantum f-divergences from retrodiction: a unifying classical variational principle
papers.authors: Francesco Buscemi
papers.problem: A classical \(f\)-divergence has several inequivalent quantum extensions. Can they all be obtained from one operational optimization?
papers.result: Yes. Compare a forward prepare-and-measure process with its reverse, obtained by Petz retrodiction relative to a reference prior \(\gamma\), subject to prescribed averages \(\rho\) and \(\sigma\). The minimum classical \(f\)-divergence between their complete records is attained by one spectral implementation, simultaneously for every operator-convex \(f\). A flat prior gives the standard (Petz) divergence, Umegaki for relative entropy. A prior equal to \(\rho\) or \(\sigma\) gives the maximal divergence, Belavkin–Staszewski for relative entropy, and power priors \(\gamma\propto\sigma^t\) give the geodesic family between them.
papers.significance: Recasts the different quantum divergences as different choices of prior for retrodiction rather than different formulas. Nussbaum–Szkoła distributions and Matsumoto’s reverse tests become optimal records of a single experiment.
papers.limitations: Finite dimension and faithful states throughout, and \(f\) must be operator convex, not merely convex. Both labels must be kept in the record; otherwise the minimum is trivially zero. The result characterizes known divergences rather than introducing new ones, and for a general prior the minimum depends on \(\gamma\), even when \(\rho=\sigma\).
description: An implementation consists of two ensembles. The states \(\tau_i\) average to \(\gamma\) under reference weights \(g_i\) and to \(\rho\) under actual weights \(a_i\); the states \(\upsilon_j\) average to \(\gamma\) and \(\sigma\) in the same way. With \(A=\gamma^{-1/2}\rho\gamma^{-1/2}\) and \(B=\gamma^{-1/2}\sigma\gamma^{-1/2}\), choosing an implementation is the same as resolving \(A=\sum_i\lambda_iE_i\) and \(B=\sum_j\mu_jH_j\) into weighted POVMs. Then \(\tau_i=\sqrt\gamma E_i\sqrt\gamma/g_i\) is the Petz retrodiction of outcome \(i\). The forward process draws \(i\), prepares \(\tau_i\) and measures \(\{H_j\}\); the reverse draws \(j\), prepares \(\upsilon_j\) and measures \(\{E_i\}\). Both report \((i,j)\), with laws \(F_{ij}=\lambda_iJ_{ij}\) and \(R_{ij}=\mu_jJ_{ij}\), where \(J_{ij}=\operatorname{Tr}[\sqrt\gamma E_i\sqrt\gamma H_j]\).

Theorem 3.1 states that, for operator-convex \(f\) with \(f(1)=0\), \[\min D_f(R\|F)=\sum_{k,l}\alpha_kf\!\left(\frac{\beta_l}{\alpha_k}\right)\operatorname{Tr}\bigl[\sqrt\gamma P_k\sqrt\gamma Q_l\bigr],\] where \(A=\sum_k\alpha_kP_k\) and \(B=\sum_l\beta_lQ_l\) are spectral decompositions. The spectral POVMs attain the minimum for every such \(f\) at once. For relative entropy the minimum is \(\operatorname{Tr}[\gamma B\log B]-\operatorname{Tr}[\sigma\log A]\). It vanishes only when \(\rho=\sigma\) and \(\rho\) commutes with \(\gamma\): equal averages with a noncommuting prior still leave distinguishable records.

The prior selects the divergence. With \(\gamma=I/d\), the minimum is the Petz divergence \(\sum_{i,j}r_if(s_j/r_i)\operatorname{Tr}[P_iQ_j]\), attained by the Nussbaum–Szkoła records \(F_{ij}=r_i|\braket{r_i}{s_j}|^2\) and \(R_{ij}=s_j|\braket{r_i}{s_j}|^2\). With \(\gamma=\rho\), \(A=I\) and the minimum is \(\operatorname{Tr}[\rho f(L)]\) with \(L=\rho^{-1/2}\sigma\rho^{-1/2}\): the maximal divergence, attained by Matsumoto’s reverse test. The prior \(\gamma_t=\sigma^t/\operatorname{Tr}\sigma^t\) gives the geodesic divergences of Capel and Costa Rico, which for relative entropy read \(D_t(\sigma\|\rho)=(1-t)\operatorname{Tr}[\sigma\log\sigma]-\operatorname{Tr}[\sigma\log(\sigma^{-t/2}\rho\sigma^{-t/2})]\).

Combining optimal implementations gives convexity at a fixed prior. For relative entropy it gives a stronger bound: \(V(\sum_kp_k\rho_k,\sigma)\le-\log\sum_kp_ke^{-V(\rho_k,\sigma)}\), obtained by letting the reverse process choose components with \(q_k\propto p_ke^{-v_k}\). The same spectral optimality holds with a channel \(\mathcal E\) inserted between preparation and measurement, with its Petz transpose in the reverse process. For channels with faithful Choi operator, the minimum coincides with a known measure of average entropy production.

methods.technique: Two operator-Jensen steps remove the implementation freedom
methods.explanation: Each weighted POVM resolution is collapsed to a function of the fixed operator it resolves, and equality holds for spectral resolutions.
math: Write \(D_f(R\|F)=\sum_i\lambda_i\operatorname{Tr}\bigl[\sqrt\gamma E_i\sqrt\gamma\sum_jf(\mu_j/\lambda_i)H_j\bigr]\). Operator Jensen for the POVM \(\{H_j\}\) gives \(\sum_jf(\mu_j/\lambda_i)H_j\ge f(B/\lambda_i)\). Expanding \(B\) spectrally leaves \(\sum_l\operatorname{Tr}\bigl[\sqrt\gamma Q_l\sqrt\gamma\sum_i\lambda_if(\beta_l/\lambda_i)E_i\bigr]\). The map \(u\mapsto uf(\beta/u)\) is operator convex, being a transpose of \(f\). A second Jensen step over \(\{E_i\}\) gives \(\sum_i\lambda_if(\beta_l/\lambda_i)E_i\ge Af(\beta_lA^{-1})\), and tracing against \(\sqrt\gamma Q_l\sqrt\gamma\ge0\) gives the bound. For spectral resolutions every operator commutes with its POVM, so both steps hold with equality.

Editorial check: for random faithful qutrit states \(\rho,\sigma,\gamma\) and \(f(u)=u\log u\), the spectral value \(2.0628\) equals the closed form of Corollary 3.2. Five hundred random admissible implementations, built by mixing a random POVM into each spectral resolution, all gave larger values, the smallest being \(2.334\).
methods.transfer: When an operational quantity is minimized over all ways of resolving fixed operators into weighted POVMs, apply operator Jensen once per resolution; spectral resolutions attain equality. The argument survives inserting a channel, as the paper shows, and should carry over to other quasi-entropies with a fixed operator sandwiched between the arguments.

methods.technique: The retrodiction prior selects the quantum divergence
methods.explanation: The same minimum, evaluated at different priors, reproduces the standard, maximal and geodesic divergences, so their differences become differences of prior.
math: Flat prior: \(A=d\rho\) and \(B=d\sigma\), and for \(f(u)=u\log u\) the minimum is \(\operatorname{Tr}[\sigma(\log\sigma-\log\rho)]\). Prior \(\rho\): \(A=I\), so only one effect is nontrivial and the value is \(\operatorname{Tr}[\rho L\log L]=\operatorname{Tr}[\sigma\log(\sigma^{1/2}\rho^{-1}\sigma^{1/2})]\), the Belavkin–Staszewski entropy. Prior \(\sigma\) gives the same value through \(\operatorname{Tr}[\sigma Kf(K^{-1})]\) with \(K=\sigma^{-1/2}\rho\sigma^{-1/2}\). Power prior: \(A_t=Z_t\sigma^{-t/2}\rho\sigma^{-t/2}\) and \(B_t=Z_t\sigma^{1-t}\); the factors \(\log Z_t\) cancel, leaving \(D_t(\sigma\|\rho)\).

Editorial check with random qutrit states: the flat prior gives \(1.3611\), equal to the Umegaki value. The priors \(\rho\) and \(\sigma\) both give \(1.6767\), equal to the Belavkin–Staszewski value in either form. At \(t=0.4\) the minimum equals Eq. (19), \(1.5832\). With \(\rho=\sigma\) and a noncommuting \(\gamma\), the minimum is \(0.338>0\), as Remark 3.3 predicts.
methods.transfer: When two quantum generalizations of a classical quantity disagree, look for a reference state that the classical derivation fixes implicitly, such as a uniform prior or one of the arguments. Making it explicit can turn separate definitions into one family indexed by the prior, so that an inequality proved once for every prior holds for every member.

papers.title: What does quantum parameter estimation estimate? A no-go result for true quantity values
papers.authors: Jacques L. Pienaar; Eran Tal; Asya Ciftci
papers.problem: Quantum metrology speaks of estimating an unknown “true value”. Is that reading consistent when the estimated quantity is itself quantum and can become entangled with the probes?
papers.result: No, not without a cost. Embedding the parameter as an observable \(\hat\theta\) reproduces standard estimation whenever its state is diagonal. But five assumptions cannot all hold together: Uniqueness, Pre-existing Value and Independence (the realist reading of a true value), Entanglement between quantity and probes, and Completeness of the quantum state (no hidden variables). Dropping any one restores consistency.
papers.significance: Shows that the interpretation-neutral appearance of parameter estimation is misleading: calling the estimate a pre-existing true value commits one to a stance on hidden variables, collapse, or the meaning of the quantum state.
papers.limitations: The argument is conceptual and uses single-parameter estimation with uncorrelated probes. Whether entanglement between a macroscopic estimand and probes is ever relevant in practice is argued by example (superconducting current superpositions), not demonstrated. The proposed escape through permutation-invariant, extendible probe states is a definitional choice.
description: Quantum parameter estimation usually treats the estimated quantity as a classical parameter \(\theta\) that controls a unitary \(U_\theta\) on probe systems; the task is to infer which value obtains. Many such quantities, such as a magnetic field produced by a current, are fundamentally quantum and could in principle be in superposition. The authors ask what happens when there is doubt whether a quantity should be modelled as a parameter or as a quantum variable, and answer by using the more general model.

The parameter is embedded in a Hilbert space: values of \(\theta\) label orthonormal states \(\ket\theta\) of a system \(A\) (binned to the precision allowed by the quantity’s definition), and the imprinting becomes a controlled unitary \(\ket\theta\ket\psi\mapsto\ket\theta U_\theta^{\otimes N}\ket\psi\). Proposition 1 shows that if \(A\) starts diagonal in this basis, the probes end in exactly the state of standard estimation, \(\sum_\theta P_0(\theta)\rho_\theta^{\otimes N}\). Proposition 2 shows that the joint output can be entangled only if \(A\) started non-diagonal.

Three assumptions express the realist reading of estimation. Uniqueness: exactly one distinguishable hypothesis about \(\theta\) is true at the end. Pre-existing Value: it was true before the probes interacted. Independence: its truth is what a sufficiently accurate measurement of \(\hat\theta\) would have shown. Two more are quantum. Entanglement: the interaction can entangle \(A\) with the probes, which partial decoherence generically allows. Completeness: if a measurement of \(\hat\theta\) would certainly give \(\theta'\), the state of \(A\) is diagonal in the \(\hat\theta\) basis. The theorem: the first three force a diagonal initial state by Completeness, which Proposition 2 makes incompatible with Entanglement.

The authors relate the result to Bell’s theorem through a form of counterfactual definiteness about an earlier, unperformed measurement of \(\hat\theta\). They show that assuming the probe state is permutation-invariant and extendible to any number of probes, as estimation tacitly does, forces separability by a de Finetti theorem, and so excludes Entanglement. They then survey the cost of rejecting each assumption in turn: hidden variables, objective collapse, many worlds, or a coherentist reading of estimates as statistical indices. The practical recommendation is to define estimation error through a posterior variance, as the latest metrology guide does, rather than through distance from a true value.

methods.technique: Embed a classical parameter as a controlling quantum register
methods.explanation: Replacing a classical control by a quantum one, with a diagonal initial state, reproduces the original model exactly; dropping diagonality then exposes what the classical model assumed.
math: With \(\sigma_{\mathrm{in}}=\sum_\theta P_0(\theta)\ketbra\theta\theta\) and \(U_{AB}=\sum_\theta\ketbra\theta\theta\otimes U_\theta^{\otimes N}\), the joint output is \[\rho_{AB}=\sum_\theta P_0(\theta)\ketbra\theta\theta\otimes\rho_\theta^{\otimes N},\] a separable state whose probe marginal is the familiar mixture. A pure superposition \(\ket\phi=\alpha'\ket{\theta'}+\alpha''\ket{\theta''}\) instead gives \(\alpha'\ket{\theta'}\ket{\psi_{\theta'}}+\alpha''\ket{\theta''}\ket{\psi_{\theta''}}\), entangled whenever the probe states differ.

Editorial remark. The probe marginal of the second case is \(|\alpha'|^2\ketbra{\psi_{\theta'}}{\psi_{\theta'}}+|\alpha''|^2\ketbra{\psi_{\theta''}}{\psi_{\theta''}}\), identical to the classical mixture. Measurements on the probes alone therefore cannot tell the two models apart. Only access to \(A\), or to correlations between \(A\) and the probes, can, which is why the paper’s escape route is a test of extendibility on joint statistics.
methods.transfer: When a model treats some quantity as a classical label, embed it as a quantum register that controls the rest of the system. Check that a diagonal initial state reproduces the old predictions, then ask what non-diagonal states would change. This isolates the assumption hidden in the classical treatment, as in analyses of quantum reference frames and of classical controls in quantum circuits.

methods.technique: Locate a no-go theorem by listing jointly inconsistent assumptions
methods.explanation: The result is stated as five assumptions that cannot all hold, each one individually droppable, so the cost of every possible interpretation is visible.
math: The chain is short. Uniqueness and Pre-existing Value give a unique hypothesis \(\theta'\) before imprinting. Independence turns it into the counterfactual “a sufficiently accurate measurement of \(\hat\theta\) would give \(\theta'\) with certainty”. Completeness turns that into a state of \(A\) diagonal in the \(\hat\theta\) basis. By Proposition 2 a diagonal state cannot become entangled with the probes, contradicting Entanglement.

Minimality matters: rejecting any one assumption gives a consistent model. Rejecting Completeness is a hidden-variable view; rejecting Entanglement by fiat is the paper’s Extendibility condition; rejecting Pre-existing Value fits collapse or Copenhagen-style accounts; rejecting Uniqueness fits many-worlds; rejecting Independence severs the link between truth and measurement.
methods.transfer: When a practice seems interpretation-neutral, write down the minimal realist assumptions it relies on and the physical assumptions of the theory, and look for a short chain to a contradiction. Showing that each assumption is individually droppable turns an impossibility result into a map of the available positions.

papers.title: Mixed State Deep Thermalization under Generic Quantum Errors
papers.authors: Xie-Hang Yu; Pavel Kos
papers.problem: After chaotic dynamics, the states of a subsystem conditioned on measuring the rest follow a universal (Haar) distribution. What distribution emerges when local errors make those conditional states mixed?
papers.result: A universal one fixed by the error alone. The late-time ensemble of conditional states is the channel-induced ensemble, \(\tilde\rho=XMX^\dagger\) with \(X\) a complex Gaussian (Ginibre) matrix and Born weight \(\operatorname{Tr}XMX^\dagger\). Here \(M\) is the normalized Choi state of the error, and only its spectrum matters. This is derived for dual-unitary circuits, global Haar dynamics and local Haar circuits at large local dimension, and checked numerically in qubit circuits and kicked Ising dynamics.
papers.significance: Extends deep thermalization to noisy dynamics. The limiting ensemble that benchmarking and shadow tomography on real hardware should assume is no longer Haar, and the measured ensemble can in principle reveal the error’s Choi spectrum even when its time and location are unknown.
papers.limitations: Analytic results assume dilute, well-separated errors and, for local circuits, large local dimension; a finite density of errors is open. Exponential convergence is derived under replica-continuation assumptions in the dual-unitary model. The numerical evidence uses two retained qubits and up to 22 measured qubits.
description: Measure the complement \(B\) of a region \(A\) after many-body dynamics. Each outcome \(\alpha\) leaves a conditional state on \(A\) with Born probability \(P_\alpha\). Their average is the reduced state of ordinary thermalization; the full ensemble, through moments \(\rho^{(k)}=\sum_\alpha P_\alpha\rho(\alpha)^{\otimes k}\), records more. For pure global states and chaotic dynamics the ensemble approaches the Haar distribution, a phenomenon called deep thermalization and observed in Rydberg and superconducting simulators. Real devices have errors, so the conditional states are mixed, and the earlier result covered only complete depolarization.

The proposed limit is defined from the error channel’s normalized Choi state \(M=(\mathrm{id}\otimes\mathcal N)(\ketbra{\phi_0}{\phi_0})\), with \(\ket{\phi_0}\) maximally entangled. Draw a \(D_A\times d^2\) Ginibre matrix \(X\) with \(\mathbb E[X^\dagger X]=I\), form \(\tilde\rho_M(X)=XMX^\dagger\) and weight it by \(P_M(X)=\operatorname{Tr}\tilde\rho_M(X)\). Several errors give \(M=\bigotimes_iM_{\mathcal N_i}\). A unitary error gives a pure \(M\) and recovers the Haar ensemble; complete depolarization gives \(M=I/d^2\) and the generalized Hilbert–Schmidt ensemble found earlier.

Because the Ginibre measure is invariant under \(X\mapsto XV\), the ensemble depends only on the eigenvalues of \(M\). Errors related by unitary rotations select the same ensemble, while channels with equal Choi purity but different spectra, such as suitable partial depolarization and partial reset, select different ones. In dual-unitary circuits the authors compute replica moments exactly and find convergence that is exponential in time, with moment-dependent prefactors that can depend on the Choi state’s input–output structure. Global Haar dynamics give typicality bounds, and local Haar circuits reduce to dominant domain walls in a permutation-space description.

Numerics in random dual-unitary circuits, local Haar circuits and a fixed kicked Ising chain, with a partial reset, a random-unitary channel and a generic four-Kraus channel, show moment distances to the predicted ensemble decaying as \(D_B^{-1/2}\). The authors propose using the measured ensemble to learn the error’s Choi spectrum, using these ensembles in place of Haar ones for randomness-based benchmarking, and extending the analysis to systems with conservation laws, where the noise-free limit is a Scrooge ensemble.

methods.technique: A random-matrix reference ensemble built from the Choi state
methods.explanation: Scrambling supplies universal Gaussian randomness, and the error channel enters only through how that randomness is mixed: \(\tilde\rho=XMX^\dagger\).
math: With \(\mathbb E[X_{a\sigma}X^*_{b\tau}]=\delta_{ab}\delta_{\sigma\tau}/D_A\), the \(k\)-th moment of the predicted ensemble is \[\rho_M^{(k)}=\int d\mu_G(X)\,P_M(X)^{1-k}\bigl(XMX^\dagger\bigr)^{\otimes k}.\] Writing \(M=V\Lambda V^\dagger\) and substituting \(X\to XV^\dagger\), which leaves the Gaussian measure unchanged, shows \(\rho_M^{(k)}=\rho_\Lambda^{(k)}\): only the Choi spectrum enters.

Editorial numerical check. One qubit kept, nine measured, a partial reset \(\rho\mapsto0.8\rho+0.2\operatorname{Tr}(\rho)\ketbra00\) between two global Haar unitaries; its Choi spectrum is about \((0.853,0.100,0.047,0)\). The simulated second moment lies at relative Hilbert–Schmidt distance 0.057 from the predicted ensemble and 0.134 from the Haar ensemble. The expected finite-size scale is \(D_B^{-1/2}\approx0.044\). Rotating \(M\) by a random unitary changed the predicted moment by 0.4%, within Monte Carlo error.
methods.transfer: When noise acts inside a scrambling process, model its late-time effect as universal Gaussian randomness contracted with the channel’s Choi state. The same construction gives reference ensembles for any procedure that assumes emergent Haar randomness, such as randomized benchmarking, shadow tomography or random-state generation, once errors are present.

methods.technique: Born-weighted moments of a projected ensemble
methods.explanation: Moments of the ensemble of conditional states can be written without normalizing each state, which makes replica calculations and numerics direct.
math: With unnormalized conditional states \(\tilde\rho(\alpha)={}_B\!\bra\alpha\rho\ket\alpha_B\) and \(P_\alpha=\operatorname{Tr}\tilde\rho(\alpha)\), \[\rho^{(k)}=\sum_\alpha P_\alpha\rho(\alpha)^{\otimes k}=\sum_\alpha P_\alpha^{1-k}\,\tilde\rho(\alpha)^{\otimes k}.\] The first moment is the reduced state; higher moments separate ensembles with the same average but different fluctuations. Distances are measured by \(\Delta^{(k)}_\xi=\|\rho^{(k)}-\rho^{(k)}_{\mathrm{ref}}\|_\xi/\|\rho^{(k)}_{\mathrm{ref}}\|_\xi\).

Editorial note on the analysis. The factor \(P_\alpha^{1-k}\) is what makes the problem non-linear. Replica methods compute moments of \(P_\alpha^{n}\tilde\rho^{\otimes k}\) for integer \(n\) and continue to \(n=1-k\); this continuation is the assumption under which the paper’s dual-unitary convergence rates hold.
methods.transfer: To compare measured ensembles of conditional states with a theory, compute Born-weighted moments directly from unnormalized conditional states and compare a few low moments in Schatten norms. This avoids sampling individual normalized states and applies to any measurement-induced ensemble.

papers.title: The limits of magic-state distillation
papers.authors: Llorenç Balada Gaggioli; Jakub Mareček
papers.problem: How few noisy T states can any stabilizer protocol, however adaptive, postselected or multistage, consume to output a magic state with error \(O(p^d)\)?
papers.result: Exact minima for small factories. Fault tolerance of any protocol reduces to projection onto a single stabilizer code, and for rational targets a fault pattern is harmful exactly when its complement is. Exhaustive search then shows: quadratic distillation of one T state needs exactly 9 inputs (a new 9-input factory is found), controlled-S needs 8, and the 8-input CCZ factory is optimal. At every order \(d\), one T state needs at least \(2d\) inputs.
papers.significance: First lower bounds that survive arbitrary postselection and adaptivity while depending strongly on \(d\). They settle the practically relevant quadratic regime, since cultivated input states already have small error.
papers.limitations: Inputs are counted per run with ideal Clifford operations, not space-time cost; per accepted output the 9-input factory consumes more inputs than the earlier 10-input protocol, since it succeeds with probability 1/128. Cubic and quartic cases keep gaps (one T state: 10–15 and 11–48). The searches are computer-assisted, and the authors report using a language model for assistance.
description: Fault-tolerant computers make Clifford operations cheap, but universality needs magic states, usually distilled from many noisy ones. Each input is \(\rho_T(p)=(1-p)\ketbra TT+pZ\ketbra TTZ\) with \(\ket T=(\ket0+e^{i\pi/4}\ket1)/\sqrt2\). A fault pattern \(e\in\mathbb F_2^n\) marks the faulty inputs, giving orthonormal pure inputs \(\ket{\phi_e}=Z^e\ket T^{\otimes n}\). A protocol has suppression order \(d\) when it accepts the fault-free input and every pattern with fewer than \(d\) faults is harmless, meaning it yields exactly the target whenever accepted. Earlier general bounds gave little beyond \(n\gtrsim d\).

Theorem 1: some stabilizer protocol tolerates a set \(H\) of patterns if and only if some stabilizer code \(C\) on the inputs, with Clifford encoding \(U\), satisfies \(\Pi_C\ket{\phi_0}\ne0\) and \(\Pi_C\ket{\phi_e}\in\mathbb C\,U\ket\tau\) for all \(e\in H\). Every tolerated input collapses onto the encoded target or is rejected. Theorem 2: flipping the sign of \(\sqrt2\) commutes with stabilizer operations, fixes targets with rational Pauli expectations such as CCZ, and sends \(\rho_T(p)\) to \(\rho_T(1-p)\). A pattern is therefore harmless exactly when its complement is, so patterns with \(|e|>n-d\) must be harmless too.

These reductions turn an unbounded space of protocols into a search over signed stabilizer codes, up to \(9\times10^{11}\) of them, tested in exact arithmetic. Results (Table 1): \(n_{\min}(T,2)=9\), \(n_{\min}(\mathrm{CS},2)=8\), \(n_{\min}(\mathrm{CCZ},2)=8\), and exact values for several first-order targets, for example six T states for CCCZ. Analytic witnesses give \(n\ge2d+1\) for rational non-stabilizer targets and \(n\ge2d\) for one T state at every order. A two-level design gives a quartic CCZ factory with 48 inputs and leading error \(864p^4\), under a third of the previous best.

The new T factory measures eight explicit 9-qubit stabilizers, postselects on all outcomes \(+1\) (probability \(1/128\) at \(p=0\)) and decodes by a Clifford, with output error \(\tfrac{27}2p^2+O(p^3)\). It lies outside the generalized triorthogonal families. The authors identify three routes to closing the remaining gaps: proving that collapsing codes contain \(Z^{\otimes n}\), stronger convex relaxations, and richer multi-level designs.

methods.technique: Reduce all protocols to one code projection
methods.explanation: Because damage is nonnegative, every accepted branch of a good protocol must itself be good, and each branch is a code projection followed by a Clifford; tolerating faults becomes a geometric collapse condition.
math: Collapse for a code \(C\): with Gram matrix \(G_{ef}=\bra{\phi_e}\Pi_C\ket{\phi_f}\), pattern \(e\) is tolerated when \(G_{00}G_{ee}=|G_{0e}|^2\), so \(\Pi_C\ket{\phi_e}\) is parallel to \(\Pi_C\ket{\phi_0}\), or when \(G_{ee}=G_{0e}=0\), so it is rejected. Worked example: measuring \(Z_1Z_2Z_3\) on \(\ket T^{\otimes3}\) succeeds with probability \(\tfrac12\). The all-faulty pattern collapses onto the fault-free vector because \(Z^{\otimes3}\) is a stabilizer, while a single fault acts as a logical Pauli and is harmful, so the order is one.

Editorial verification of Proposition 7. The eight listed stabilizers commute; projecting \(\ket T^{\otimes9}\) onto the code gives acceptance probability exactly \(1/128\). For each of the nine single faults, \(\Pi_CZ_i\ket T^{\otimes9}\) is either zero or parallel to \(\Pi_C\ket T^{\otimes9}\). The identity of Proposition 3, \(\mathrm{CS}_{12}\mathrm{CS}_{13}\ket{{+}{+}{+}}=\mathrm{CX}_{23}H_2\mathrm{CX}_{12}S_2H_2\ket{\mathrm{CCZ}}\), also holds, with overlap 1.
methods.transfer: When optimizing over adaptive, postselected protocols with a nonnegative failure measure, check whether each accepted branch must already succeed. If so, the optimum is attained by one branch, which often has a rigid normal form such as a code projection, Kraus operator or measurement, and the search becomes finite.

methods.technique: Galois conjugation pairs complementary faults
methods.explanation: The field automorphism \(\sqrt2\mapsto-\sqrt2\) maps noisy T states with error \(p\) to error \(1-p\) while fixing every stabilizer operation and every rational target, which doubles the set of patterns a protocol must tolerate.
math: \(\rho_T(p)=\tfrac12\bigl[I+\tfrac{1-2p}{\sqrt2}(X+Y)\bigr]\), so \(\sigma:\sqrt2\mapsto-\sqrt2\) sends \(\rho_T(p)\) to \(\rho_T(1-p)\), and hence \(\rho_e\) to \(\rho_{e+\mathbf1}\). Stabilizer branches act on Pauli coefficients by rational matrices, so they commute with \(\sigma\). For a target with rational Pauli expectations, the damages of \(e\) and \(e+\mathbf1\) are \(\sigma\)-conjugates in \(\mathbb Q(\sqrt2)\), and one vanishes exactly when the other does.

Consequence (editorial phrasing). With order \(d\), all patterns with \(|e|<d\) and all with \(|e|>n-d\) must be harmless. For small \(n\) this forces a witness state, built only from harmless patterns, to be converted into the target by stabilizer operations, which is impossible. This gives \(n\ge2d+1\) for rational targets that are not stabilizer states.
methods.transfer: When inputs and allowed operations have entries in a number field, look for field automorphisms that commute with the operations. They map one physical situation to another, here \(p\leftrightarrow1-p\), and any property preserved by the automorphism must hold in both, often halving a search or yielding a lower bound.

papers.title: Size-independent Logarithmic Sobolev Inequalities for Quantum Gibbs Samplers
papers.authors: Hongrui Chen; Zhiyan Ding; Jianfeng Lu
papers.problem: Does relative entropy decay at a rate independent of system size under quasi-local quantum Gibbs samplers for non-commuting Hamiltonians?
papers.result: Yes, in two regimes. For the Gaussian KMS Gibbs sampler, both the \(L^2\) logarithmic Sobolev inequality and the modified one (MLSI) hold with system-size-independent constants: in one dimension at every finite temperature, and in any fixed dimension at sufficiently high temperature. This gives \(O(\log n+\log(1/\epsilon))\) mixing time.
papers.significance: Removes the logarithmic losses of earlier one-dimensional MLSI bounds, gives the first MLSI for non-commuting spin systems at high temperature in arbitrary dimension, and shows that a gradient-flow structure is not needed for size-independent entropy decay.
papers.limitations: Covers one specific sampler, the Gaussian KMS one, under local mixing and local energy conditions that are verified only in the two stated regimes. Constants depend on temperature, range and local dimension and are not optimized. Concurrent work proves the one-dimensional result by a different method.
description: Gibbs samplers are Lindblad dynamics \(e^{t\mathcal L_*}\) whose fixed point is a thermal state \(\sigma_\beta\propto e^{-\beta H}\). They are algorithms for preparing thermal states on quantum computers and models of thermalization. The MLSI with constant \(\alpha_1\) is equivalent to \(D(e^{t\mathcal L_*}\rho\|\sigma)\le e^{-2\alpha_1t}D(\rho\|\sigma)\). A constant independent of the number \(n\) of sites gives mixing in time logarithmic in \(n\). For commuting Hamiltonians such results use spatial factorization of entropy, which fails for non-commuting ones. For KMS-symmetric samplers of non-commuting systems, earlier bounds lost factors of \(1/\log n\) or worse.

The route goes through the \(L^2\) logarithmic Sobolev inequality, \(\alpha_2\,\mathrm{Ent}_{2,\sigma}(X)\le\mathcal E_{2,\sigma}(X)\), which controls the sandwiched Rényi-2 divergence. Rewritten on the doubled Hilbert space it reads \(D(Y^2\|\sigma_\beta)\le C_\beta\bra Y(-\mathsf L_{\sigma_\beta})\ket Y\) for unit-norm Hermitian \(Y\), comparing an entropy with an energy of the sampler’s parent Hamiltonian. At infinite temperature the sampler is single-site depolarizing and the inequality holds with an explicit constant \(C_0\).

The inequality is transported from \(s=0\) to \(s=\beta\) along a unitary path \(\mathsf U_s\) carrying the infinite-temperature Gibbs vector to the one at \(s\), a quantum analogue of Moser’s transport. If the entropy and energy change along the path by at most \(C_S\) and \(C_E\) times the energy, Grönwall’s inequality gives \(C_\beta=(C_0+\beta C_S)e^{\beta C_E}\). The generator of the path solves Poisson and Sylvester equations. Its quasi-locality, under local rapid-mixing and local energy conditions, makes \(C_S\) and \(C_E\) independent of system size, and the conditions are verified in one dimension and at high temperature.

Rényi-2 decay is converted into relative-entropy decay without loss by a tensor-power argument (Theorem 3.3). If a channel contracts the Rényi-2 divergence by the same factor \(a\) on every number \(m\) of copies, including correlated inputs, it contracts relative entropy by \(a\). The proof combines \(D\le\tilde D_2\le D_{\max}\) with the quantum asymptotic equipartition property. Because the sampler on \(m\) copies is the sampler of a Hamiltonian in the same class, the rate is uniform in \(m\).

methods.technique: Transport a functional inequality along a unitary path
methods.explanation: Prove the inequality where it is easy (infinite temperature, product state) and carry it to the target by a path along which entropy and energy change only in proportion to the energy.
math: Let \(E_s=\bra{Y_s}(-\mathsf L_{\sigma_s})\ket{Y_s}\) with \(\ket{Y_s}=\mathsf U_s\ket{Y_0}\). Assume \(|\tfrac{d}{ds}D(Y_s^2\|\sigma_s)|\le C_SE_s\) and \(|\tfrac{d}{ds}E_s|\le C_EE_s\). The second gives \(E_s\le e^{(\beta-s)C_E}E_\beta\), since \(e^{C_Es}E_s\) is nondecreasing. Integrating the first and using \(D(Y_0^2\|\sigma_0)\le C_0E_0\), \[D(Y_\beta^2\|\sigma_\beta)\le C_0E_0+C_S\int_0^\beta E_s\,ds\le(C_0+\beta C_S)e^{\beta C_E}E_\beta.\]

Because \(\mathsf U_\beta\) is unitary and preserves Hermiticity, every unit-norm Hermitian \(Y\) is some \(Y_\beta\), so \(\alpha_2(\mathcal L_\beta)\ge2e^{-\beta C_E}/(C_0+\beta C_S)\). Editorial remark: all of the system-size dependence is pushed into \(C_S\) and \(C_E\), which is why quasi-locality of the path generator is the crux of the paper.
methods.transfer: To prove a uniform inequality for a family of models indexed by a parameter such as temperature, coupling or time, find a norm-preserving transport between them and bound the logarithmic derivatives of both sides of the inequality along it. Grönwall then delivers the inequality at the endpoint with explicit constants.
